title: Harp: Leveraging Quasi-Sequential Characteristics to Accelerate Sequence-to-Graph Mapping of Long Reads
problem: Sequence-to-graph (S2G) mapping incurs high graph processing overheads and creates new performance hotspots that differ from traditional sequence-to-sequence mapping. Current software implementations and hardware accelerators struggle with the computational demands of S2G mapping for genomic long reads.
motivation: S2G mapping represents a paradigm shift in computational genomics with superior accuracy, but its widespread adoption is hindered by substantial performance challenges that limit practical applicability.
method: Harp works by recognizing that sequence-to-graph mapping—the process of aligning long genomic reads to a reference graph (a network of genetic sequences)—tends to access the graph in a quasi-sequential pattern, mostly moving forward with occasional deviations rather than random jumps. The system exploits this pattern through optimized dataflow and scheduling that arrange computations to match these natural access patterns. This reduces graph processing overhead compared to approaches that treat all accesses as random.
key_novelty: Harp identifies and exploits quasi-sequential (mostly-forward with occasional jumps) access patterns in graph-based long-read mapping to reduce graph processing overhead.
contributions: Characterizes performance hotspots in sequence-to-graph mapping showing overhead shift from S2S paradigm
Proposes Harp system exploiting quasi-sequential characteristics for S2G acceleration
Demonstrates efficiency gains for mapping long reads using graph-based approach
Addresses hardware and software implementation challenges of S2G mapping
limitations: Limitations and generalizability beyond long-read genomics not discussed in abstract.
